items.stem: State what is meant by the term "data logger".
items.answer: An electronic device that records measurements from sensors (e.g. O₂, CO₂, pH, temperature) at set intervals over time
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: an electronic device that records measurements from sensors (e.g. O₂, CO₂, pH, temperature) at set intervals over time. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain how to calibrate an eyepiece graticule and use it to measure a cell.
items.answer: Place stage micrometer on the stage; line up graticule and micrometer scales; count how many micrometer divisions correspond to a number of graticule divisions; calculate the length of one graticule division (e.g. 25 × 10 µm/100 = 2.5 µm); replace with specimen; count graticule divisions across the cell; multiply.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Place stage micrometer on the stage; line up graticule and micrometer scales; count how many micrometer divisions correspond to a number of graticule divisions; calculate the length of one graticule division (e.g. 25 × 10 µm/100 = 2.5 µm); replace with specimen; count graticule divisions across the cell; multiply. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: With reference to separating chloroplast pigments by thin-layer chromatography, explain how it illustrates chromatography.
items.answer: Carotene runs near the solvent front, while chlorophyll b travels least. Different pigments have different solubilities and attraction to the stationary phase, giving different Rf values.
items.markingKey: Context (Carotene runs near the solvent front, while chlorophyll b travels least.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Different pigments have different solubilities and attraction to the stationary phase, giving different Rf values. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to chromatography.

items.stem:
An oxygen probe connected to a data logger recorded the dissolved oxygen concentration (mg dm⁻³) in a sealed flask containing germinating peas at 25 °C.

Time / min | Dissolved O₂ / mg dm⁻³
0 | 8.96
2 | 8.03
4 | 7.1
6 | 6.17
8 | 5.24
10 | 4.31
12 | 4.26

(a) State the oxygen concentration at 6 minutes. [1]
(b) Calculate the mean rate of oxygen uptake between 0 and 10 minutes. [2]
(c) Explain why oxygen concentration decreases. [1]
items.answer: (a) 6.17 mg dm⁻³ (b) 0.465 mg dm⁻³ min⁻¹ (c) The germinating peas respire aerobically, using oxygen as the final electron acceptor.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Digital sensors and data loggers always give better data than manual methods."
items.answer: Data loggers improve precision and quantity of data, but only when correctly calibrated and suited to the measurement.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: many readings at precise intervals reduce random error; remove human reading errors. Arguments against: probes must be calibrated and can drift; some measurements, such as identifying species, still need human skill. Supported judgement: Data loggers improve precision and quantity of data, but only when correctly calibrated and suited to the measurement.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A scale in the eyepiece of a microscope, with arbitrary units, which must be calibrated against a stage micrometer"?
items.answer: eyepiece graticule
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of eyepiece graticule.

items.stem: Sofia writes: "Rf values can be greater than 1." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Substances cannot move further than the solvent front, so Rf is between 0 and 1.
items.markingKey: Substances cannot move further than the solvent front, so Rf is between 0 and 1. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using the ×10 objective, 40 eyepiece graticule divisions lined up with 26 stage micrometer divisions (1 division = 10 µm). A cell measured 46 eyepiece divisions. Calculate the value of one eyepiece division and the actual length of the cell.
items.answer: 6.50 µm per division; 299.0 µm

items.stem: In a chromatogram the solvent front moved 10.1 cm and a pigment moved 8.1 cm from the origin. What is the Rf value?
Describe how microscopy, chromatography and sampling techniques are used in biological investigations, and explain how to ensure that data are reliable.
items.answer: Graticule calibration, measurement, magnification; Rf; quadrats and transects; random sampling; data loggers; repeats; controls; calibration; sample size.
items.markingKey: Graticule calibration, measurement, magnification; Rf; quadrats and transects; random sampling; data loggers; repeats; controls; calibration; sample size.

items.stem: How many different values of the independent variable are generally recommended for an IA investigation showing a trend?
items.answer: at least five
items.markingKey: at least five. To establish a relationship.

items.stem: Explain the importance of risk assessment and ethics in biological investigations.
items.answer: Identify hazards (chemicals, microorganisms, heat, sharp tools) and control measures (goggles, aseptic technique, lower temperatures); ethical issues: avoid harming animals, minimise disturbance to habitats, informed consent and anonymity for human subjects, safe disposal.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Identify hazards (chemicals, microorganisms, heat, sharp tools) and control measures (goggles, aseptic technique, lower temperatures); ethical issues: avoid harming animals, minimise disturbance to habitats, informed consent and anonymity for human subjects, safe disposal. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Kwame writes: "A hypothesis is just a guess." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: A hypothesis is a testable prediction based on scientific reasoning.
items.markingKey: A hypothesis is a testable prediction based on scientific reasoning. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A 1 : 10 serial dilution of a 1 % starch solution is performed three times. What is the final concentration?
A student has a 1 mg cm⁻³ stock solution of caffeine. Calculate the volumes of stock and distilled water needed to make 10 cm³ of each of: 0.1, 0.2, 0.6, 0.8 mg cm⁻³.
items.answer: 0.1 mg cm⁻³: 1 cm³ stock + 9 cm³ water; 0.2 mg cm⁻³: 2 cm³ stock + 8 cm³ water; 0.6 mg cm⁻³: 6 cm³ stock + 4 cm³ water; 0.8 mg cm⁻³: 8 cm³ stock + 2 cm³ water
items.markingKey: C₁V₁ = C₂V₂, so V₁ = C₂V₂/C₁ (M1); 0.1 mg cm⁻³: 1 cm³ stock + 9 cm³ water; 0.2 mg cm⁻³: 2 cm³ stock + 8 cm³ water; 0.6 mg cm⁻³: 6 cm³ stock + 4 cm³ water; 0.8 mg cm⁻³: 8 cm³ stock + 2 cm³ water (A1 for each two correct, max A2).

items.stem:
A student investigated the effect of temperature on the time taken for amylase to digest starch (iodine end-point). Each temperature was tested three times. The stopwatch uncertainty is ±0.5 s.

Temperature / °C | Trial 1 / s | Trial 2 / s | Trial 3 / s | Mean / s
20 | 176 | 176 | 158 | 170.0
30 | 94 | 89 | 83 | 88.7
40 | 58 | 56 | 54 | ?
50 | 70 | 61 | 67 | 66.0
60 | 146 | 136 | 148 | 143.3

(a) Calculate the mean time at 40 °C. [1]
(b) Calculate the rate (1000/mean time) at 40 °C and at 20 °C. [2]
(c) Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the mean time at 40 °C due to the stopwatch. [1]
(d) State a conclusion from these data. [2]
items.answer: (a) 56.0 s (b) 17.9 and 5.9 s⁻¹ (c) 0.9 % (d) Rate increases with temperature up to about 40 °C (optimum), then decreases at higher temperatures.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Laboratory experiments are more useful than field investigations in biology."
items.answer: Both are needed: laboratory experiments establish causes, while field investigations test whether these apply in natural conditions.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: variables can be controlled, so causal relationships can be established; easier to replicate. Arguments against: field studies are more realistic and show natural interactions; some questions (e.g. ecology) cannot be studied in the lab. Supported judgement: Both are needed: laboratory experiments establish causes, while field investigations test whether these apply in natural conditions.

items.stem:
A student measured the heart rate (beats min⁻¹) of Daphnia in pond water and in 1 % caffeine.

Sample | caffeine | pond water
1 | 349 | 314
2 | 295 | 302
3 | 307 | 303
4 | 344 | 294
5 | 367 | 305
6 | 293 | 285

(a) Calculate the mean for caffeine. [1]
(b) Calculate the standard deviation of each sample. [2]
(c) State a null hypothesis for a t-test on these data. [1]
(d) A t-test gives t = 1.88. Determine the degrees of freedom and, using a critical value of 2.23 at p = 0.05, state a conclusion. [2]
items.answer: (a) 325.8 (b) caffeine 31.4; pond water 9.9 (c) There is no significant difference between the mean for caffeine and the mean for pond water. (d) df = 10; t < critical value – accept H₀; no significant difference

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The variable that is deliberately changed by the investigator"?
items.answer: independent variable
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of independent variable.

items.stem: Why might a temperature-controlled water bath be used in an enzyme experiment?
options: Temperature affects enzyme activity, so it must be controlled to avoid confounding the results.
It speeds up the reaction always.
items.answer: Temperature affects enzyme activity, so it must be controlled to avoid confounding the results.
items.markingKey: C. Control variable.

items.stem: Distinguish between dependent variables and independent variables.
items.answer: The independent variable is changed by the investigator; the dependent variable is measured in response.
items.markingKey: The independent variable is changed by the investigator; the dependent variable is measured in response. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between dependent variables and independent variables.
items.answer: The independent variable is changed by the investigator; the dependent variable is measured in response.
items.markingKey: The independent variable is changed by the investigator; the dependent variable is measured in response. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: In an investigation of the effect of temperature on the rate of respiration of yeast, measured by CO₂ bubbles per minute, what is the dependent variable?
options: number of CO₂ bubbles per minute
items.answer: number of CO₂ bubbles per minute
items.markingKey: C. The dependent variable is what is measured: number of CO₂ bubbles per minute.

items.stem: Outline one way in which an IA on the effect of caffeine on Daphnia heart rate shows designing a valid investigation.
items.answer: Daphnia are placed in caffeine solutions of different concentrations and heart rate is counted under a microscope. The temperature of water must be controlled and animals returned unharmed, showing control of variables and ethical practice.
items.markingKey: Context (Daphnia are placed in caffeine solutions of different concentrations and heart rate is counted under a microscope.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The temperature of water must be controlled and animals returned unharmed, showing control of variables and ethical practice. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to designing a valid investigation.

items.stem: Describe how to plan a scientific investigation in biology, including variables, method, safety and ethics.
items.answer: Research question; background and hypothesis; IV with range and intervals; DV and method of measurement; controlled variables and how; control; repeats; pilot study; data table; risk assessment; ethical and environmental considerations; statistical analysis planned.
items.markingKey: Research question; background and hypothesis; IV with range and intervals; DV and method of measurement; controlled variables and how; control; repeats; pilot study; data table; risk assessment; ethical and environmental considerations; statistical analysis planned.

items.stem: What value of p is usually taken as the threshold for significance in biology?
items.markingKey: 0.05. 5 % probability that results are due to chance.

items.stem: Why is p = 0.05 used as a threshold?
options: It means there is less than a 5 % probability that the result is due to chance.
It means 95 % of data are correct.
items.answer: It means there is less than a 5 % probability that the result is due to chance.
items.markingKey: A. Convention.

items.stem: Why does a strong correlation not prove a causal relationship?
options: Another factor could cause both, or the relationship may be coincidental.
r is always zero for causes.
items.answer: Another factor could cause both, or the relationship may be coincidental.
items.markingKey: A. Correlation ≠ causation.

items.stem: Ana counted the number of bubbles released per minute by a pondweed in repeated trials. The values of bubble count (bubbles min⁻¹) were: 33, 23, 28, 29, 34. Calculate the mean and the standard deviation.
items.answer: mean = 29.4 bubbles min⁻¹; SD = 4.4 bubbles min⁻¹
items.markingKey: Mean = Σx/n = 147/5 = 29.4 bubbles min⁻¹ (A1); SD (sample, n − 1) = 4.4 bubbles min⁻¹ (A1). Accept population SD 3.9.

items.stem: Which statistic would best test whether light intensity and plant height are related?
items.answer: Pearson correlation coefficient
items.markingKey: B. Two continuous variables.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Statistical tests are essential in every biological investigation."
items.answer: Statistical tests are essential when conclusions depend on comparing variable data, but they must be chosen and interpreted correctly.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they distinguish real effects from chance variation; allow objective conclusions. Arguments against: qualitative investigations or very large effects may not need them; tests can be misused if assumptions are not met. Supported judgement: Statistical tests are essential when conclusions depend on comparing variable data, but they must be chosen and interpreted correctly.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "standard deviation"?
options: A measure of the spread of values around the mean; about 68 % of values in a normal distribution lie within ±1 SD
A consistent error in the same direction in all measurements, such as an uncalibrated instrument; not reduced by repeats
The absolute uncertainty divided by the measured value, multiplied by 100
How close repeated measurements are to each other
items.answer: A measure of the spread of values around the mean; about 68 % of values in a normal distribution lie within ±1 SD
items.markingKey: A. "standard deviation" is a measure of the spread of values around the mean; about 68 % of values in a normal distribution lie within ±1 SD.

items.stem: Distinguish between the t-test and the chi-squared test.
items.answer: The t-test compares the means of two samples of continuous data; the chi-squared test compares observed and expected frequencies of categorical data.
items.markingKey: The t-test compares the means of two samples of continuous data; the chi-squared test compares observed and expected frequencies of categorical data. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain how a t-test is used to compare two sets of data.
items.answer: State null hypothesis (no significant difference between means); calculate means and SDs; calculate t; degrees of freedom = n₁ + n₂ − 2; compare with critical value at p = 0.05; if t > critical value reject H₀ — the difference is significant; assumptions: approximately normal data, similar variance, independent samples.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: State null hypothesis (no significant difference between means); calculate means and SDs; calculate t; degrees of freedom = n₁ + n₂ − 2; compare with critical value at p = 0.05; if t > critical value reject H₀ — the difference is significant; assumptions: approximately normal data, similar variance, independent samples. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Zara writes: "r = 0 means there is no relationship at all." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: r = 0 means no linear relationship; a non-linear relationship may still exist.
items.markingKey: r = 0 means no linear relationship; a non-linear relationship may still exist. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe smoking and lung cancer studies in the 1950s and explain what it reveals about correlation and causation.
items.answer: Doll and Hill found a strong positive correlation between smoking and lung cancer. Correlation alone did not prove causation, but consistency, dose–response and biological mechanisms later established causation.
items.markingKey: Context (Doll and Hill found a strong positive correlation between smoking and lung cancer.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Correlation alone did not prove causation, but consistency, dose–response and biological mechanisms later established causation. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to correlation and causation.

items.stem: Explain how statistical analysis is used to draw conclusions from biological data, with reference to standard deviation, the t-test and correlation.
items.answer: Mean; SD and error bars; normal distribution; t-test: null hypothesis, df, critical value, conclusion; correlation: r, r², scatter graphs; correlation vs causation; sample size; significance level.
items.markingKey: Mean; SD and error bars; normal distribution; t-test: null hypothesis, df, critical value, conclusion; correlation: r, r², scatter graphs; correlation vs causation; sample size; significance level.

items.stem: Which is an example of a systematic error?
items.answer: a balance that reads 0.05 g when empty
items.markingKey: a balance that reads 0.05 g when empty. Consistent offset.

items.stem: Why does using a larger quantity reduce percentage uncertainty?
options: It increases accuracy of the instrument.
The absolute uncertainty stays the same while the measured value increases.
items.answer: The absolute uncertainty stays the same while the measured value increases.
items.markingKey: C. %U = U/value × 100.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain how to write an effective conclusion for an IA.
items.answer: State the relationship found between IV and DV, with reference to processed data (means, trends, statistical test results); state whether the hypothesis is supported; explain the trend using scientific theory; compare with published values; acknowledge uncertainty and the limits of the conclusion. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: State the relationship found between IV and DV, with reference to processed data (means, trends, statistical test results); state whether the hypothesis is supported; explain the trend using scientific theory; compare with published values; acknowledge uncertainty and the limits of the conclusion. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: With reference to an IA on the effect of temperature on lipase activity using phenolphthalein, explain how it illustrates evaluating limitations.
items.answer: Students found it difficult to judge exactly when the pink colour disappeared. Subjective end-points introduce random error; a pH probe or colorimeter would improve precision.
items.markingKey: Context (Students found it difficult to judge exactly when the pink colour disappeared.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Subjective end-points introduce random error; a pH probe or colorimeter would improve precision. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to evaluating limitations.

items.stem: A value of 70 mm was measured with a ruler with an uncertainty of ±0.5 mm. Calculate the percentage uncertainty.
Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "The evaluation is the most important section of an IA report."
items.answer: The evaluation is important, but it depends on good design and analysis; all sections are interdependent.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: shows understanding of the reliability and validity of the data; improvements and extensions show scientific thinking. Arguments against: without a sound research design and analysis there is nothing worth evaluating; all criteria contribute to the final mark. Supported judgement: The evaluation is important, but it depends on good design and analysis; all sections are interdependent.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "precision".
items.answer: How close repeated measurements are to each other
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: how close repeated measurements are to each other. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Lukas writes: "A conclusion should claim that the hypothesis has been proven." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Data can support or refute a hypothesis, but not prove it.
items.markingKey: Data can support or refute a hypothesis, but not prove it. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Why should a conclusion include a scientific explanation?
options: It removes the need for evaluation.
It links the observed trend to biological theory, showing why the relationship occurs.
items.answer: It links the observed trend to biological theory, showing why the relationship occurs.
items.markingKey: D. Explanation.

items.stem: Five repeat measurements of the time (s) for a colour change were: 57.1, 23.3, 60.9, 60.7, 57.7. Identify the anomalous result, and calculate the mean with and without it. State which mean should be used and why.
items.answer: anomaly 23.3 s; mean with it 51.9 s, without it 59.1 s; use 59.1 s because the anomaly does not fit the pattern and is likely due to error (repeat if possible)
items.markingKey: Anomaly identified (A1); means 51.9 and 59.1 (A1); justification (R1).

items.stem: A balance reads 0.02 g with nothing on it. All masses are therefore:
options: too high by 0.02 g – a systematic error
items.answer: too high by 0.02 g – a systematic error
items.markingKey: A. Zero error.

items.stem: Explain how the analysis, conclusion and evaluation sections of a biology IA should be written.
items.answer: Processing raw data (means, SD, rates, % change); graphs with error bars; statistical tests; uncertainty propagation; conclusion linked to RQ, hypothesis and theory; evaluation: strengths, limitations with effects, realistic improvements, extensions.
items.markingKey: Processing raw data (means, SD, rates, % change); graphs with error bars; statistical tests; uncertainty propagation; conclusion linked to RQ, hypothesis and theory; evaluation: strengths, limitations with effects, realistic improvements, extensions.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "dependent variable".
items.answer: The variable that is measured, which is expected to change in response to the independent variable
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the variable that is measured, which is expected to change in response to the independent variable. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The proportion of the variation in one variable that is explained by its linear relationship with the other"?
items.answer: coefficient of determination (r²)
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of coefficient of determination (r²).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A suggested further investigation that builds on the findings of the original one"?
items.answer: extension
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of extension.

items.stem: Why must an eyepiece graticule be calibrated?
options: Its divisions have no fixed size in the specimen plane; their value depends on the objective lens magnification.
It is always 1 µm per division.
items.answer: Its divisions have no fixed size in the specimen plane; their value depends on the objective lens magnification.
items.markingKey: A. Calibration.

items.stem: "A control experiment is the same as a controlled variable." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: A control is a comparison condition; controlled variables are kept constant throughout.
items.markingKey: A control is a comparison condition; controlled variables are kept constant throughout. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain how the standard deviation is used to describe and compare data sets.
items.answer: SD measures spread around the mean; small SD means data are clustered and reliable; about 68 % within ±1 SD, 95 % within ±2 SD; error bars of ±1 SD on graphs; overlapping error bars suggest a difference may not be significant; a t-test is needed to confirm.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: SD measures spread around the mean; small SD means data are clustered and reliable; about 68 % within ±1 SD, 95 % within ±2 SD; error bars of ±1 SD on graphs; overlapping error bars suggest a difference may not be significant; a t-test is needed to confirm. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between precision and accuracy.
items.answer: Accuracy is how close a measurement is to the true value; precision is how close repeated measurements are to each other.
items.markingKey: Accuracy is how close a measurement is to the true value; precision is how close repeated measurements are to each other. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between belt transects and line transects.
items.answer: A line transect records organisms touching a line at intervals; a belt transect uses quadrats placed along the line, giving abundance data over a wider strip.
items.markingKey: A line transect records organisms touching a line at intervals; a belt transect uses quadrats placed along the line, giving abundance data over a wider strip. items.stem: Explain how to design a valid investigation into the effect of pH on the activity of an enzyme.
items.answer: IV: pH using buffers at at least five values (e.g. 3–9); DV: rate (e.g. time for starch to disappear, O₂ volume per minute); controlled: temperature (water bath), enzyme and substrate concentration and volume, time; control without enzyme; at least three repeats; calculate means and SD.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: IV: pH using buffers at at least five values (e.g. 3–9); DV: rate (e.g. time for starch to disappear, O₂ volume per minute); controlled: temperature (water bath), enzyme and substrate concentration and volume, time; control without enzyme; at least three repeats; calculate means and SD. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student measured the reaction time (ms) of students before and after a sleepless night (different students). After no sleep: 257, 243, 325, 334, 286, 282. Well rested: 221, 215, 263, 230, 274, 235. Calculate the mean and standard deviation of each sample. A t-test gives t = 2.73; the critical value for 10 degrees of freedom at p = 0.05 is 2.23. items.answer: after no sleep: mean 287.8, SD 36.1; well rested: mean 239.7, SD 23.6; t > critical value – significant difference, reject H₀
items.markingKey: Means (A1); SDs (A1); comparison of 2.73 with 2.23 (M1); correct conclusion about H₀ (A1).

items.stem: "Digital sensors and data loggers always give better data than manual methods." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Data loggers improve precision and quantity of data, but only when correctly calibrated and suited to the measurement.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: many readings at precise intervals reduce random error; remove human reading errors. Arguments against: probes must be calibrated and can drift; some measurements, such as identifying species, still need human skill. Supported judgement: Data loggers improve precision and quantity of data, but only when correctly calibrated and suited to the measurement. Markbands (8 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "dependent variable"?
options: The variable that is measured, which is expected to change in response to the independent variable
A square frame of known area used to sample organisms in a habitat
A value between −1 and +1 that measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two variables
A microscope slide with an accurately ruled scale (often 1 mm divided into 100 divisions of 10 µm) used to calibrate an eyepiece graticule
items.answer: The variable that is measured, which is expected to change in response to the independent variable
items.markingKey: A. "dependent variable" is the variable that is measured, which is expected to change in response to the independent variable.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "correlation coefficient (r)".
items.answer: A value between −1 and +1 that measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two variables
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a value between −1 and +1 that measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two variables. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "percentage uncertainty"?
options: An experimental condition used for comparison, in which the independent variable is absent or at a standard level
An electronic device that records measurements from sensors (e.g. O₂, CO₂, pH, temperature) at set intervals over time
The absolute uncertainty divided by the measured value, multiplied by 100
Lines on a graph showing variability (e.g. ±1 SD or range) of the data at each point
items.answer: The absolute uncertainty divided by the measured value, multiplied by 100
items.markingKey: C. "percentage uncertainty" is the absolute uncertainty divided by the measured value, multiplied by 100.

items.stem: Explain the difference between magnification and resolution.
items.answer: Magnification is how many times larger the image is than the object; resolution is the ability to distinguish two points close together as separate.
items.markingKey: Magnification is how many times larger the image is than the object; resolution is the ability to distinguish two points close together as separate. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Why are repeats carried out at each value of the independent variable?
options: To identify anomalies and calculate a mean, improving reliability.
items.answer: To identify anomalies and calculate a mean, improving reliability.
items.markingKey: B. Reliability.

items.stem: A student claims: "If two error bars overlap, the difference is definitely not significant." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Overlap suggests it may not be significant, but a statistical test is needed to decide.
items.markingKey: Overlap suggests it may not be significant, but a statistical test is needed to decide. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "A conclusion should claim that the hypothesis has been proven." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Data can support or refute a hypothesis, but not prove it.
items.markingKey: Data can support or refute a hypothesis, but not prove it. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain how chromatography is used to separate and identify photosynthetic pigments.
items.answer: Grind leaves with solvent to extract pigments; spot concentrated extract on origin line drawn in pencil; place in solvent below origin; solvent moves up carrying pigments at different rates depending on solubility and attraction to paper; measure distances; calculate Rf; compare with known values.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Grind leaves with solvent to extract pigments; spot concentrated extract on origin line drawn in pencil; place in solvent below origin; solvent moves up carrying pigments at different rates depending on solubility and attraction to paper; measure distances; calculate Rf; compare with known values. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between controlled variables and a control.
items.answer: A control is a separate condition used for comparison (e.g. no enzyme); controlled variables are factors kept constant in all conditions.
items.markingKey: A control is a separate condition used for comparison (e.g. no enzyme); controlled variables are factors kept constant in all conditions. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student recorded light intensity (lux) and number of plant species in quadrats: (487, 7); (587, 6); (676, 3); (760, 0); (843, 3); (943, 7); (968, 11). Calculate Pearson’s correlation coefficient r and r², and interpret the result.
items.answer: r = 0.24; r² = 0.06; weak positive correlation – 6 % of variation explained; does not prove causation
items.markingKey: r = 0.24 (A1); r² = 0.06 (A1); interpretation of strength/direction (A1); correlation ≠ causation (R1).

items.stem: Using an IA on the effect of temperature on lipase activity using phenolphthalein as an example, explain evaluating limitations.
items.answer: Students found it difficult to judge exactly when the pink colour disappeared. Subjective end-points introduce random error; a pH probe or colorimeter would improve precision.
items.markingKey: Context (Students found it difficult to judge exactly when the pink colour disappeared.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Subjective end-points introduce random error; a pH probe or colorimeter would improve precision. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to evaluating limitations.

items.stem: Using the ×40 objective, 100 eyepiece graticule divisions lined up with 37 stage micrometer divisions (1 division = 10 µm). A cell measured 6 eyepiece divisions. Calculate the value of one eyepiece division and the actual length of the cell.
items.answer: 3.70 µm per division; 22.2 µm

items.stem: In an investigation of the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis of Elodea, measured by O₂ volume per minute, which of these should be a controlled variable?
options: volume of O₂ produced per minute
the colour of the student’s pen
items.answer: NaHCO₃ concentration
items.markingKey: B. NaHCO₃ concentration could affect the dependent variable, so it must be kept constant.

items.stem: Briefly describe comparing stomatal density on sun and shade leaves and explain what it reveals about the t-test.
items.answer: Students counted stomata on 10 leaves of each type and used a t-test to compare means. A t value greater than the critical value showed that sun leaves have significantly more stomata.
items.markingKey: Context (Students counted stomata on 10 leaves of each type and used a t-test to compare means.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: A t value greater than the critical value showed that sun leaves have significantly more stomata. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the t-test.

items.stem: Five repeat measurements of the time (s) for a colour change were: 43.4, 44.3, 42.5, 67.7, 44.2. Identify the anomalous result, and calculate the mean with and without it. State which mean should be used and why.
items.answer: anomaly 67.7 s; mean with it 48.4 s, without it 43.6 s; use 43.6 s because the anomaly does not fit the pattern and is likely due to error (repeat if possible)
items.markingKey: Anomaly identified (A1); means 48.4 and 43.6 (A1); justification (R1).

items.stem: A student claims: "Data loggers make controls unnecessary." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: They improve measurement, but controlled variables and controls are still needed for a valid experiment.
items.markingKey: They improve measurement, but controlled variables and controls are still needed for a valid experiment. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
A student measured the heart rate (beats min⁻¹) of Daphnia in pond water and in 1 % caffeine.

Sample | caffeine | pond water
1 | 324 | 308
2 | 319 | 316
3 | 350 | 252
4 | 327 | 272
5 | 347 | 273
6 | 331 | 313
7 | 375 | 304

(a) Calculate the mean for caffeine. [1]
(b) Calculate the standard deviation of each sample. [2]
(c) State a null hypothesis for a t-test on these data. [1]
items.answer: (a) 339.0 (b) caffeine 19.6; pond water 25.1 (c) There is no significant difference between the mean for caffeine and the mean for pond water.

items.stem: "Statistical tests are essential in every biological investigation." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Statistical tests are essential when conclusions depend on comparing variable data, but they must be chosen and interpreted correctly.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they distinguish real effects from chance variation; allow objective conclusions. Arguments against: qualitative investigations or very large effects may not need them; tests can be misused if assumptions are not met. Supported judgement: Statistical tests are essential when conclusions depend on comparing variable data, but they must be chosen and interpreted correctly. Markbands (7 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "The evaluation is the most important section of an IA report."
items.answer: The evaluation is important, but it depends on good design and analysis; all sections are interdependent.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: shows understanding of the reliability and validity of the data; improvements and extensions show scientific thinking. Arguments against: without a sound research design and analysis there is nothing worth evaluating; all criteria contribute to the final mark. Supported judgement: The evaluation is important, but it depends on good design and analysis; all sections are interdependent. Markbands (7 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: Explain how to calculate the actual size and magnification of a specimen using an eyepiece graticule and a stage micrometer.
items.answer: Calibration; value of one division; measurement in divisions; actual size; magnification = image/actual; scale bars; units µm and mm.
items.markingKey: Calibration; value of one division; measurement in divisions; actual size; magnification = image/actual; scale bars; units µm and mm.
